Gauracharya) IN CRIMINAL APPEAL No. 124/2025 U/s 415 BNSS Date of institution : 27.01.2024 Date when judgment reserved : 26.05.2026 Date of Judgment : 30.05.2026 DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 2 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. IN CRIMINAL APPEAL No. 487/2025 U/s 415 BNSS Date of institution : 06.10.2025 Date when judgment reserved : 26.05.2026 Date of Judgment : 30.05.2026 COMMON JUDGMENT 1. INTRODUCTORY: THE WEIGHT OF A PAPER INSTRUMENT 1.1. Law, in its finest hour, is not a sword wielded with the fury of vengeance, but a balance held with the patient hands of justice. In the theatre of commercial relations, where promises are made tangible by the humble cheque -- that rectangular slip of paper which, has become the very bloodstream of modern commerce -- the dishonour of a cheque is not merely a financial event; it is a breach of trust, a silent declaration that the word given was hollow. Chapter XVII of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 , enacted as a statutory sentinel of commercial morality, speaks in unequivocal terms: let those who issue cheques know that the law shall not look the other way when those instruments return dishonoured like unpaid debts boomeranging against the conscience of the drawer. 1.2. And yet, justice is a two-edged instrument. The very provisions that protect the creditor must be administered with scrupulous faithfulness to their precise legislative architecture. A court of justice is not a court of emotion. It neither swings to the drum of righteous indignation when a complainant who has been defrauded demands the blood of the convict, nor DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 3 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. does it yield to the sentimental appeal of a mother of two who pleads poverty. It weighs. It measures. It decides. And it must decide within the four corners of the law -- not a cubit beyond. 1.3. Before this Court have come two cross-appeals -- one filed by the complainant Ms. Amazon Distributors Pvt. Ltd. (Criminal Appeal No. 124/2025) and the other by the convict-accused Smt. Sushma (Criminal Appeal No. 487/2025) -- both directed against the judgment dated 22.01.2025 and the order on sentence dated 31.01.2025 passed by the Ld. JMFC NI Act-01, PHC, New Delhi in Complaint Case No. 13540/2019 under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Both appeals, after due consideration, are found to be without merit, and this Court proceeds to dismiss both, for the reasons that follow. 2. BRIEF FACTS OF THE CASE 2.1. The seeds of this litigation were sown in the soil of commercial betrayal. Ms. Amazon Distributors Pvt. Ltd. (hereinafter the "complainant company"), a distributor of products of Kellogg's and P&G, had engaged one Sh. Parveen -- husband of the respondent Smt. Sushma -- as a Sales Executive from 06.10.2018. His duties were straightforward: procure orders, ensure delivery to customers, collect payments, and deposit them with the complainant company. 2.2. What unfolded, however, was a brazen conspiracy. Sh. Parveen, in league with certain co-employees namely Ms. Megha, Mr. Rajeev Saini, Mr. Anil Goel, and Mr. Chintu Giri, began booking fake orders in the names of different customers, diverting the delivered goods to his own godown, DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 4 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. affixing forged stamps on invoices to simulate legitimate deliveries, and then replacing genuine customer cheques with his own personal cheques -- and the cheques of his wife, the present convict-accused Smt. Sushma -- bearing fake customer stamps on their reverse. The total amount defalcated from the complainant company in this conspiracy is admitted to be Rs. 22,24,019/-, with Sh. Parveen himself acknowledging in his own handwriting vide an admission letter dated 07.07.2019 that he had cheated a sum of Rs. 23,64,091/-, out of which goods worth Rs. 2,23,000/- were recovered. 2.3. In discharge of the aforesaid liability, the accused Smt. Sushma issued a cheque bearing No. 000007, dated 13.07.2019, for a sum of Rs. 1,28,294/- drawn on HDFC Bank, D.B. Gupta Road, Dev Nagar, New Delhi, in favour of the complainant company. When the said cheque was presented for encashment at Citi Bank, DLF Capital Point, Baba Kharak Singh Marg, New Delhi, it was returned dishonoured vide cheque return memo dated 16.07.2019 bearing the ignominious remark: "Payment Stopped by Drawer." A legal demand notice dated 09.08.2019 was duly issued and served upon the accused on 13.08.2019 as evidenced by the postal receipts and the tracking report, the address of the accused being admitted by her. No payment was forthcoming within the statutory period of fifteen days, and accordingly, the complainant company filed a complaint case under Section 138 of the NI Act before the competent court, which was instituted on 25.09.2019. 2.4. It is relevant to note that the complainant company had filed a total of 17 complaint cases under the NI Act against the accused Smt. Sushma DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 5 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. and her husband Sh. Parveen in connection with 17 dishonoured cheques, aggregating to approximately Rs. 22 lacs. The present case concerns one such cheque. 3. PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE TRIAL COURT 3.1. The complaint, duly supported by a pre-summoning evidence affidavit of the Authorised Representative (AR) of the complainant company Sh. Bajrang Singh Shekhawat, was taken up by the competent court. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, only the accused no. 1, namely Smt. Sushma, was summoned vide order dated 11.02.2020, her husband Sh. Parveen (accused no. 2) not having been summoned. 3.2. Upon appearance of the accused, notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C. was served upon her on 23.01.2023. She pleaded not guilty. At this stage, she made a significant admission: A) she admitted to being the drawer of the cheque in question and to her signatures thereon. B) She, however, claimed that the cheque had been given in a blank signed condition to her husband, and that she was unaware of the purpose for which he had used it. 3.3. Admission and denial of documents under Section 294 Cr.P.C. was conducted, whereby the accused admitted the genuineness and correctness of the original cheque (Ex. CW-1/5) and the bank return memo (Ex. CW-1/6), consequent whereupon two bank witnesses were dropped. DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 6 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. 3.4. The AR of the complainant company was examined on affidavit at the post-summoning stage, and was subjected to extensive cross-examination. 3.5. The accused chose not to lead any defence evidence. 3.6. Final arguments were heard on 29.11.2024, and written submissions were filed on behalf of both sides. Vide separate judgment dated 22.01.2025, the Ld. Trial Court convicted Smt. Sushma under Section 138 NI Act. The matter was then posted for arguments on sentence, which were heard on 31.01.2025. 4. THE IMPUGNED JUDGMENT AND ORDER ON SENTENCE 4.1. The Conviction A) The Ld. Trial Court, in its well-considered judgment dated 22.01.2025, traversed the legal framework under Section 138 NI Act with precision, setting out the six essential ingredients to be established by the complainant. The court noted that once the execution of the cheque is admitted by the accused, the presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 NI Act are automatically triggered -- a principle firmly established by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar , (2019) 4 SCC 197, cited by the trial court -- wherein it was held that upon admission of signatures on the cheque, the court is bound to raise presumption under Section 139 NI Act. B) The accused had raised a two-fold defence: i. first, non-receipt of the legal demand notice; and ii. second, absence of any legally enforceable debt or liability. DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 7 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. C) The Ld. Trial Court, upon careful consideration, rejected both. On the first, relying upon the admission of the accused as to her correct address on the notice and the evidence of postal receipts, the court invoked the presumption of due delivery under Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act and Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, further fortifying the conclusion by reference to C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 6 SCC 555. D) On the second limb of defence -- the "security cheque" plea -- the Ld. Trial Court, after a thorough discussion, held that merely labelling a cheque as a "security cheque" does not, by itself, constitute a rebuttal of the statutory presumption under Section 139 NI Act. Reliance was placed on Sampelly Satyanarayana Rao v. Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Ltd. , (2016) 10 SCC 458, Sunil Todi v. State of Gujarat, (2021) SCC OnLine SC 1174, and Sripati Singh v. State of Jharkhand, (2021) SCC OnLine SC 1002. The accused having neither entered the witness box nor adduced any defence evidence, and her oral assertions having been found to be bald, vague, and wholly unsubstantiated by any cogent or reliable evidence, the court found that the accused had failed to rebut the mandatory presumptions as per law, even on the lower standard of preponderance of probabilities. In a finding that resonates with common sense as much as with law, the court held: "The entire defence of the accused is nothing but a set of bald, vague assertions put together which are unsubstantiated by any cogent or reliable evidence." The accused Smt. Sushma was accordingly convicted under Section 138 NI Act. DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 8 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. 4.2. The Order on Sentence A) Vide order on sentence dated 31.01.2025, the Ld. Trial Court, after hearing the submissions of both sides and taking into account the mitigating circumstances -- the accused being a mother of two minor children, her poor economic condition, and her responsibility for the entire family including an elderly father-in-law -- as well as the compensatory and restitutive object of Chapter XVII NI Act as underscored in R. Vijayan v. Baby , ( 2012) 1 SCC 260, Meters Instruments Pvt. Ltd. v. Kanchan Mehta , ( 2018) 1 SCC 560, and P. Mohanraj v. Shah Brothers Ispat Pvt. Ltd. , (2021) 6 SCC 258, exercised its judicial discretion in favour of imposing only a fine and no sentence of imprisonment. The accused was directed to pay a fine of Rs. 1,70,000/- (Rupees One Lakh Seventy Thousand only) to the complainant as compensation within 90 days from the date of the order, under the benevolent provisions of Section 357(3) Cr.P.C., with recovery thereof to be made under Section 421 Cr.P.C. in case of default. Notably, no default imprisonment was awarded in case of non-payment of the fine/compensation. 5. THE TWO CROSS-APPEALS As this Court has already noted, two appeals stand before it -- both directed against the aforesaid judgment and order on sentence -- one by each side. By a notable coincidence of grievances, the complainant says the punishment is too lenient, and the convict says the conviction itself is wrong. This Court, therefore, takes them up seriatim. DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 9 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. 5.1. Criminal Appeal No. 124/2025 -- The Complainant's Appeal (Amazon Distributors Pvt. Ltd.) -- DISMISSED AS NOT MAINTAINABLE A) The Prayer Clause i. Before proceeding to the merits of this appeal, it is necessary to reproduce the prayer clause, as it is this very prayer that seals its fate. The prayer in Criminal Appeal No. 124/2025 reads: "It is therefore prayed that this Ld. Court may be pleased to set aside the order on sentence dated 31.01.2025 passed by the court of Ms. Poonam Singh, Ld. JMFC, Patiala House Court, Delhi, in CC No. 13540/2019 and accused may kindly be punished with rigorous maximum imprisonment as provided for the offence." ii. The prayer, therefore, is not for enhancement of compensation. It is not for conviction in a higher offence. It is squarely, unambiguously, and exclusively for the imposition of maximum rigorous imprisonment of two years -- the maximum sentence prescribed for an offence under Section 138 of the NI Act. The character of this prayer is the key to the maintainability of the appeal. B) The Legal Framework i. The proviso to Section 372 Cr.P.C. (and the corresponding proviso to the relevant section under the BNSS, which is Section 413 BNSS 1) reads, to the extent material: "Provided that the victim shall have a right to prefer an appeal against any order passed by the Court acquitting the accused or convicting for a lesser offence or imposing inadequate compensation." 1 413. No appeal to lie unless otherwise provided. No appeal shall lie from any judgment or order of a Criminal Court except as provided for by this Sanhita or by any other law for the time being in force: Provided that the victim shall have a right to prefer an appeal against any order passed by the Court acquitting the accused or convicting for a lesser offence or imposing inadequate compensation, and such appeal shall lie to the Court to which an appeal ordinarily lies against the order of conviction of such Court. DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 10 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. ii. The language of the proviso is exhaustive, not illustrative. The Legislature has conferred upon the victim three, and only three, grounds for an appeal: (a) acquittal of the accused, (b) conviction for a lesser offence, and (c) imposition of inadequate compensation. iii. The Legislature has deliberately omitted "inadequate sentence" from the victim's armoury of appellate remedies under Section 372/413 BNSS. This is no drafting oversight; it is a considered legislative choice. C) Arguments Of The Complainant/Appellant Learned counsel for the complainant argued that the accused is a habitual offender -- there are 17 cases against her and her husband -- and that the Ld. Trial Court has taken a wholly lenient view unwarranted by the gravity of the offence. It was further argued that no imprisonment was awarded at all, and that the object of Section 138 NI Act, which is deterrent as well as compensatory, demands that maximum rigorous imprisonment ought to have been imposed. D) Arguments of the Convict/Respondent Learned counsel for the respondent-convict countered that the present appeal, being an appeal for enhancement of substantive sentence, is not maintainable under the proviso to Section 372 Cr.P.C./413 BNSS, as the complainant does not qualify as a "victim" entitled to challenge the adequacy of sentence as distinct from adequacy of compensation. The distinction between the two, it was argued, is one of fundamental legal DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 11 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. significance. An appeal for inadequate compensation is permissible; an appeal for inadequate punishment is not. E) Observations And Decision i. This Court is in complete agreement with the contentions of the respondent-convict on the question of maintainability. It is settled law -- settled by the highest court of the land -- that the remedy of appeal is a creature of statute, and no appeal can be preferred except on grounds and in the manner provided by law. ii. The Hon'ble Division Bench of the Delhi High Court, speaking in Pravinder Kansal v. State (NCT of Delhi ), 2019 SCC OnLine Del 11508, decided on 27.11.2019, categorically reiterated the following: "An appeal by the victim under Section 372 CrPC, is not maintainable if it only challenges the order on sentence on the ground that it imposes inadequate punishment." iii. The position of law, as further articulated by Hon'ble Full Bench in the Parvinder Kansal vs The State Of Nct Of Delhi AIR 2020 Supreme Court 4044, is that the victim's right of appeal under the proviso to Section 372 is restricted to three eventualities -- acquittal, conviction for a lesser offence, and imposition of inadequate compensation. The power to prefer an appeal for inadequate sentence is vested in the State Government under Section 377 Cr.P.C., and no such right inheres in the victim/complainant. iv. The relevant para is reproduced as under: "9. Chapter XXIX of the Code of Criminal Procedure , 1973 deals with 'Appeals' and Section 372 makes it clear that no appeal to lie unless otherwise provided by the Code or any other law for the time being in force. It is not in dispute that in the instant case appellant has preferred appeal only under Section 372 , Cr.PC. The proviso is inserted to Section 372 , Cr.PC by DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 12 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Act 5 of 2009. Section 372 and the proviso which is subsequently inserted read as under: "372. No appeal to lie unless otherwise provided. - No appeal shall lie from any judgment or order of a Criminal Court except as provided for by this Code or by any other law for the time being in force: Provided that the victim shall have a right to prefer an appeal against any order passed by the Court acquitting the accused or convicting for a lesser offence or imposing inadequate compensation, and such appeal shall lie to the Court to which an appeal ordinarily lies against the order of conviction of such Court." A reading of the proviso makes it clear that so far as victim's right of appeal is concerned, same is restricted to three eventualities, namely, acquittal of the accused; conviction of the accused for lesser offence; or for imposing inadequate compensation. While the victim is given opportunity to prefer appeal in the event of imposing inadequate compensation, but at the same time there is no provision for appeal by the victim for questioning the order of sentence as inadequate, whereas Section 377 , Cr.PC gives the power to the State Government to prefer appeal for enhancement of sentence. While it is open for the State Government to prefer appeal for inadequate sentence under Section 377 , Cr.PC but similarly no appeal can be maintained by victim under Section 372 , Cr.PC on the ground of inadequate sentence. It is fairly well settled that the remedy of appeal is creature of the Statute. Unless same is provided either under Code of Criminal Procedure or by any other law for the time being in force no appeal, seeking enhancement of sentence at the instance of the victim, is maintainable. Further we are of the view that the High Court while referring to the judgment of this Court in the case of National Commission for Women v. State of Delhi & Anr. (2010) 12 SCC 599 has rightly relied on the same and dismissed the appeal, as not maintainable." v. In the present case, the complainant-appellant Ms. Amazon Distributors Pvt. Ltd. is not challenging an acquittal. It is not challenging a conviction for a lesser offence. It is not challenging the adequacy of compensation -- indeed, the fine of Rs. 1,70,000/- imposed by the trial court is, if anything, higher than the cheque amount of Rs. 1,28,294/-. What the complainant is challenging is the absence of rigorous imprisonment. That is a challenge to the adequacy of the substantive sentence -- a ground that is not available to a complainant/victim under Section 372 Cr.P.C./413 BNSS DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 13 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. vi. In the opinion of this Court, this appeal is not maintainable under the proviso to Section 372 Cr.P.C. or under the corresponding provision of Section 415(3) BNSS. The legislature, in its wisdom, has not given the private complainant the right to seek enhancement of the substantive sentence. That power belongs to the State. The appeal filed by Amazon Distributors Pvt. Ltd. is accordingly dismissed as not maintainable, without going into the merits thereof. 5.2. Criminal Appeal No. 487/2025 -- The Convict's Appeal (Smt. Sushma) -- DISMISSED ON MERITS A) The Application for Condonation of Delay -- Allowed i. Smt. Sushma, through her learned counsel Sh. H.M. Gauracharya, Advocate, preferred the present criminal appeal under Section 415 BNSS read with Section 374(3) Cr.P.C., challenging both the judgment of conviction dated 22.01.2025 and the order on sentence dated 31.01.2025 passed by, Ld. JMFC NI Act-01, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, in Complaint Case No. 13540/2019 under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The appeal was initially presented on 21.02.2025 and thereafter, upon its registration and allocation, came to be assigned to this Court on 06.10.2025. ii. An application for condonation of delay was filed, placing on record the explanation that the delay in the formal filing/re-filing of the appeal was caused by technical objections at the filing counter and procedural requirements of the e-filing process, and was neither deliberate, wilful, nor intended to defeat the ends of justice. DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 14 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. iii. This Court has considered the application on its own merits. The explanation offered is not implausible, and the conduct of the appellant -- who applied for the certified copies on 15.02.2025, the day after the order on sentence -- demonstrates a promptness inconsistent with any intention to delay. Furthermore, and this is a consideration that weighs significantly with this Court, the complainant-company itself has filed a cross-appeal, which is also pending before this Court for decision. Where a cross-appeal is filed and is to be decided simultaneously, the interest of comprehensive adjudication and the avoidance of piecemeal justice demand that the convict's appeal also be decided on its merits. To dismiss the convict's appeal on the ground of delay alone while deciding the complainant's cross-appeal would be a procedural incongruity that this Court is not prepared to countenance. The application for condonation of delay is accordingly allowed for the reasons stated therein, and more so because the counter-appeal is also pending before this Court and requires a comprehensive adjudication. The delay stands condoned. B) The Impugned Judgment and Order on Sentence: Before taking up the grounds of challenge, it is necessary to briefly recapitulate the core findings of the Ld. Trial Court, so that the grounds of challenge may be appreciated in their proper context. i. The Ld. Trial Court found that: (a) the accused Smt. Sushma had admitted her signatures on the cheque in question bearing No. 000007 dated 13.07.2019 for Rs. 1,28,294/-, drawn on her HDFC Bank account; DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 15 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. (b) she had admitted the genuineness and correctness of the cheque and the bank return memo; (c) the cheque was dishonoured with the remark "Payment Stopped by Drawer"; (d) the legal demand notice was properly addressed and sent to the accused's admitted address, and the presumption of service stood established under Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act read with Section 27 of the General Clauses Act; (e) no payment was made within the statutory period of fifteen days; (f) the presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act stood triggered by the admission of the signature; (g) the accused failed to rebut those presumptions by cogent evidence -- she neither entered the witness box nor led any defence evidence; and (h) the "security cheque" defence was found to be wholly unsubstantiated by evidence and therefore insufficient to displace the statutory presumptions. ii. The Ld. Trial Court, in its order on sentence, directed the convict to pay a fine of Rs. 1,70,000/- (Rupees One Lakh Seventy Thousand only) to the complainant as compensation within 90 days, under Section 357(3) Cr.P.C., without imposing any sentence of imprisonment, and further without imposing any default sentence for non-payment of the fine. Recovery in case of default was left to Section 421 Cr.P.C. DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 16 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. iii. It is against this composite judgment and order that the present appeal has been preferred by the convict. C) The Grounds of Appeal Learned counsel for the appellant-convict has raised the following grounds in the appeal memorandum as well as in the additional written arguments filed on 26.05.2026, which are taken up and addressed individually and in groups. i. Impugned Judgment Based on Conjecture and Surmise; Failure to Appreciate Evidence (a) This is a general ground of challenge that pervades every appeal against conviction and, by itself, without specific identification of the particular piece of evidence that has been misread or the particular legal principle that has been violated, does not advance the cause of the appellant. However, it shall be examined in the context of the specific factual grievances that follow. (b) The Ld. Trial Court's judgment is not a document of conjecture. It is grounded in the admitted facts -- the admitted signature, the admitted dishonour, the admitted address -- and in the robust legal architecture of Sections 118(a) and 139 NI Act, interpreted in light of a long line of authoritative Supreme Court precedent. The criticism of conjecture is unsustainable when the findings of fact are based on admissions of the accused herself. A finding that rests upon the accused's own admissions is not a finding of surmise; it is the most direct and incontrovertible form of factual determination known to law. This ground fails. DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 17 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. ii. Failure to Appreciate the Contradictions in the Deposition of CW-1 (a) The argument is that Ld. Trial Court failed to appreciate the facts on record particularly in the notice issued by the complainant respondent in which the complainant clearly mentioned -- "That you have usurped/cheated a sum of Rs. 22,24,019/-(twenty two lacs twenty four thousand nineteen only) from my client in conspiracy with above-said accomplices, wherein you addressee no 1 is also seemed to be involved as you issued one post dated cheque (appellant)" -- and the Trial Court failed to consider the cross of the AR of the complainant that 'I have never personally met the accused/appellant prior to the institution of the present case', while wrongly mentioning that he had talked to the accused over phone call through her husband Parveen, though the complainant failed to mention the said facts about the phone call with the accused/appellant in his complaint. (b) The argument, stripped to its core, is this: the AR of the complainant company admitted in cross-examination that he had never personally met the accused Smt. Sushma prior to the institution of the case, and that the phone call he mentioned having had with the accused was through her husband -- a fact not mentioned in the complaint. This, it is argued, creates doubt about the nature of the accused's involvement. (c) This Court has carefully perused the deposition of CW-1 Sh. Bajrang Singh Shekhawat, Finance Manager and AR of the complainant company. In the cross-examination conducted on DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 18 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Appeal No. 487/2025 M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. Sushma Vs. Vs. Sushma M/s Amazon Distributors (P) Ltd. 19.07.2024, the witness stated: "I have never personally met the accused prior to institution of the present case. Vol. I have talked to the accused over phone call through her husband Praveen. I have not mentioned the fact about the phone call with the accused in my complaint." (d) The omission of the telephone conversation from the complaint is noted. However, this omission is of no material significance to the case against the accused under Section 138 NI Act. The case under Section 138 NI Act does not rest upon any personal meeting between the AR and the accused. It rests upon a specific, finite chain: the issuance of a cheque by the accused, its dishonour, the issuance of a demand notice, the failure to pay. None of these links in the chain depend upon whether the AR had personally met the accused or had spoken to her over the phone. A cheque is a negotiable instrument; it is presented to the bank by the payee's banker -- not by the AR in person. A demand notice is dispatched to the address of the drawer -- not delivered in a personal visit. The prosecution's case does not require the AR to have met the accused; and the fact that he had not met her does not weaken the documentary evidence that constitutes the foundation of the prosecution. (e) As for the assertion in the legal notice that the accused was "also seemed to be involved" -- the language of the notice, however tentative, is not a statement of the prosecution's case. (b) Once the execution of the cheque -- i.e., the fact that the cheque bears the signature of the accused and was issued from the accused's account -- is admitted or proved, the court is bound to presume, under Section 118(a) NI Act, that the cheque was made for consideration, and under Section 139 NI Act, that the cheque was issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. ( Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar , (2019) 4 SCC 197) (c) These presumptions are rebuttable, but the burden of rebuttal lies upon the accused. The accused must rebut the presumption on a preponderance of probabilities -- a standard lower than proof beyond reasonable doubt, but still requiring the raising of a probable defence. Bald denial, unsubstantiated assertions, and unsupported submissions in written arguments do not discharge this burden. ( Rangappa v. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441; K.N. Beena v. Muniyappan , (2001) 8 SCC 458) (d) The accused may discharge the burden either by leading positive evidence of her own, or in exceptional cases, from the case of the complainant itself -- from the averments in the complaint, from the statutory notice, or from the evidence adduced in cross- examination. However, for the accused to successfully use the complainant's own evidence to discharge the burden, the cross- examination must affirmatively establish facts inconsistent with DLND010015252025 DLND010082832025 Page 34 of 38 Crl Appeal No. 124/2025 Crl. Even if it is proved that the cheque was issued as security, it must further be established that no legally enforceable debt or liability had accrued or crystallised as on the date of issue or presentation of the cheque. (Sampelly Satyanarayana Rao v. IREDA, (2016) 10 SCC 458; Sunil Todi v. State of Gujarat , (2021) SCC OnLine SC 1174) (f) The accused choosing not to enter the witness box and not to lead any defence evidence is a circumstance that a court may take into consideration, though it cannot itself be a basis for drawing an adverse inference against the accused in a criminal trial. However, where the only defence raised is one of pure denial and the defence version is not supported by any documentary evidence, the failure to enter the witness box significantly impairs the rebuttal of the presumption. (g) Applying each of these principles to the facts of the present case, this Court is satisfied that the Ld. Trial Court arrived at the correct conclusion.
